For most brands, a TikTok Shop agency scales GMV faster than a first in-house hire, because the agency already has the process, the creator relationships, and the reps, while a new hire is learning on your budget. In-house wins on control and long-term cost once you are big enough to keep a specialist fully busy and sharp. The right answer depends on your stage.

The case for an agency

  • Speed. An agency runs a proven process from day one: recruiting, seeding, management, ads. No ramp.
  • Expertise. They do TikTok Shop all day across brands, so they have seen what works in your category. A single hire only knows what they have personally done.
  • No hiring risk. Recruiting and training a good creator manager is hard and slow. An agency is a switch you flip.
  • Accountability. A good agency ties fees to GMV. A salaried hire is paid regardless.

The case for in-house

  • Control. Full ownership of strategy and daily decisions.
  • Long-term cost. At high volume, a salaried specialist can be cheaper than a percentage of large GMV.
  • Deep brand knowledge. An in-house person lives your product and can move fast on brand nuance.
  • Always available. No shared attention across an agency's client roster.

Side by side

Agency In-house hire
Ramp time Immediate Weeks to months
Expertise Broad, cross-brand Limited to one person
Cost Retainer / commission Salary + overhead
Control Shared Full
Hiring risk None High
Best stage Launch and scaling Large, steady volume

Why this is a full-time job either way

Whichever you choose, someone has to run a real daily loop. One seller described it as "1 to 3 hero products, a strong TikTok-exclusive offer, competitive creator commissions, consistent sample outreach, clear hooks, not rigid scripts" (@jordantwestecom on X). That is a job, not a side task. The agency-vs-in-house question is really: who runs that loop, and do they already know how?

The hidden problem with a first hire

Most brands cannot keep a creator manager both busy and expert early on. The role is either underused (you are paying full-time for part-time work) or in over their head (one person cannot match an agency's cross-brand pattern recognition). The economics of a single hire only work once your program is big enough to justify and sharpen the role.

The practical path

Many brands use an agency to build and scale the program, learn what works, then bring it in-house once volume justifies a dedicated team, sometimes hiring the very playbook the agency proved. That sequence gets you speed now and control later. If you are still deciding between a hire, a tool, and an agency, read DIY, software, or agency.

The takeaway

Agency for speed, expertise, and no hiring risk while you scale. In-house for control and cost once you are big enough to keep a specialist fully productive. Match the choice to your stage, not to a preference.

Want to scale GMV without a hire? Book a call, or find the creators a program would target.
